And, "This is the will of God, your sanctity, that you abstain from fornication, that each one know how to possess his own vessel in sanctity and honour, not in the passion of lust, like the nations which know not God." What do the Galatians read? "Manifest are the works of the flesh." What are these? In the first place he set fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, "which I foretell you, as I have foretold, that they who do such things shall not obtain by inheritance the kingdom of God." But what do the Romans learn more than not to forsake the Lord after the faith? "What then shall we say? Do we persevere in delinquency, that grace may abound? Far from it. We who are dead to delinquency, how shall we yet live in it? Or are you ignorant that we who have been baptized into Christ have been baptized into his death? We are therefore buried with him through baptism into death, that, as Christ rose from the dead, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been buried together in the likeness of his death, we shall be also of his resurrection — knowing this, that our old man is fastened to the cross with him. But if we are dead with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, raised from the dead, dies now no more; death shall no more have dominion over him. For in that he died to delinquency, he died once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So you too reckon yourselves dead indeed to delinquency, but living to God through Christ Jesus." Therefore, Christ having died once, no one who has died to delinquency after Christ — and especially to so great a delinquency — can come to life again. Or, if fornication and adultery can again be admitted, Christ too will be able to die again. But the Apostle urges, forbidding delinquency to reign in our mortal body — whose weakness of the flesh he knew. "For as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity, so now present them servants to justice unto sanctity." For although he denied that any good dwells in his flesh, yet it was according to the law of the letter, in which he was; but according to the law of the spirit, to which he attaches us, he frees us from the weakness of the flesh. "For the law," he says, "of the spirit of life has set you free from the law of delinquency and death." For although he may seem in part to dispute out of Judaism, yet he directs toward us the integrity and fullness of the disciplines, on account of whom, labouring under the law, God sent his Son through flesh in the likeness of the flesh of delinquency, and for delinquency condemned delinquency in the flesh, "that the right of the law," he says, "might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit. For they who walk according to the flesh savour the things of the flesh; and they who according to the spirit, the things of the spirit." But he affirmed the mind of the flesh to be death; thereafter, both enmity, and that against God; and that those who are in the flesh — that is, in the mind of the flesh — cannot please God; and, "If you live according to the flesh," he says, "it shall come to pass that you die." But what do we understand by the mind of the flesh and the life of the flesh, except whatever it is shameful to pronounce? For the other things of the flesh the Apostle too would have named. Accordingly, to the Ephesians too, reckoning up their former state, he warns of the future: "In which we too were conversant, doing the lusts and pleasures of the flesh." Marking, in short, those who had denied themselves — Christians, namely — in that they had handed themselves over to the working of all uncleanness, "But you," he says, "have not so learned Christ." And again he says thus: "Let him who stole steal no more." But also, "Let him who committed adultery hitherto commit adultery no more; and let him who fornicated hitherto fornicate no more." For he would have added these too, if he had been wont to hold out pardon to such, or had been at all willing that it should be held out — he who, unwilling to be polluted even by a word, says, "Let no foul speech proceed out of your mouth." Likewise, "But let fornication and all uncleanness not even be named among you, as becomes saints" — so far is it from being excused — "knowing this, that no fornicator or unclean person has the kingdom of God. Let no one seduce you with empty words; for on account of these things comes the wrath of God upon the sons of unbelief." Who seduces with empty words, but he who harangues that adultery is remissible — not regarding even its foundations dug out by the Apostle, when he checks drunkennesses and revellings, as also here: "And be not drunk with wine, in which is riot"? He shows to the Colossians too what members they should mortify upon earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil concupiscence, and foul talk. Now concede to so many and such sentences that one thing which you hold. Few things are overshadowed by many, doubtful by certain, obscure by manifest. Even if for certain the Apostle had forgiven that Corinthian his fornication, it would be another matter — something he once did against his own institution, by reason of the time. He circumcised Timothy alone, and yet abolished circumcision.

"But these things," he says, "will pertain to the interdiction of all unchastity and the addiction to all modesty, the place of pardon being nevertheless preserved — which is not at once denied if offences are condemned, since the time of pardon may concur with the condemnation which excludes it." It followed that the Psychics should savour this too; and therefore we have reserved for this place those things which have anciently been provided, openly, for the denying of ecclesiastical communion in causes of this kind. For in the Proverbs too of Solomon — which we call paroimiai — concerning the adulterer specifically, as nowhere expiable, he says, "But the adulterer, through want of senses, acquires the perdition of his own soul; he sustains pains and dishonours. And his ignominy shall not be abolished for ever. For the indignation, full of jealousy, will not spare the man in the day of judgement." If you have thought this said of the heathen, surely you have already heard concerning the faithful, through Isaiah, "Go out from the midst of them, and be separated, and touch not the unclean thing." You have at once in the Psalms, "Blessed is the man who has not gone away in the counsel of the impious, nor stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pestilence." Whose voice too afterward: "I have not sat with the assembly of vanity, and with those who act unjustly I will not enter in" — this of the Church of evildoers — "and with the impious I will not sit"; and, "I will wash my hands with the innocent, and will compass your altar, O Lord" — that he may be alone rather than many — since indeed, "With the holy you shall be holy, and with the innocent man innocent, and with the elect elect, and with the perverse perverse." And elsewhere: "But to the sinner God says, Why do you set forth my justifications, and take my testament into your mouth? If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you set your portion." Hence therefore the Apostle too, being informed, says, "I wrote to you in the epistle, not to mix with fornicators" — surely not the fornicators of this world — and the rest, "for then you ought to go out of the world. But now I write to you, if anyone named a brother among you be a fornicator or an idolater" (for what so conjoined?) "or a defrauder" (for what so near?) and the rest, "with such not even to take food," much less the Eucharist; since, namely, a little leaven too makes the whole lump distasteful. Likewise to Timothy: "Lay hands hastily on no one, neither communicate with the sins of others." Likewise to the Ephesians: "Do not therefore be partakers with them; for you were once darkness." And yet more pressingly: "Do not communicate with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather even reprove them. For the things that are done by them in secret it is shameful even to utter." What is more shameful than unchastities? But if he denounces to the Thessalonians that they should withdraw even from a brother walking idly, how much more from a fornicator? For these things have been resolved by Christ, who loves his Church, who gave himself for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the laver of water in the word, that he might present to himself a glorious Church, having no spot or wrinkle — surely after the laver — but that she should be holy and without reproach; thereafter, namely, without the wrinkle of age, as a virgin; without the spot of fornication, as a bride; without the reproach of vileness, as one cleansed. What, if here too you should conceive to answer, that communion is indeed taken away from sinners, especially from those polluted in the flesh, but for the present — to be restored, namely, from the suit of penitence, according to that clemency of God which prefers the penitence of the sinner to his death? For this foundation of your opinion must everywhere be battered. We say therefore that, if it had befitted the divine clemency to provide a demonstration of itself even to those fallen after the faith, the Apostle would so have said: "Do not communicate with the works of darkness, unless they shall have done penitence"; and, "With such not even to take food, unless after they shall have wiped off the boots of the brethren by rolling"; and, "He who violates the temple of God, God will violate him, unless he shall have shaken off the ashes of all hearths in the Church from his head." For he ought to have determined what he had condemned — to what point, and under what condition, he had condemned it — if he had condemned with a temporal and conditional and not a perpetual severity. Now since in all his epistles he both forbids such a one to be admitted after the faith, and thrusts the admitted from communion, without hope of any condition or time, he assists rather our view, showing that the Lord prefers that penitence which is before the faith, which is before baptism, to be held better than the death of the sinner — of one to be washed once for all by the grace of Christ, of one who once for all died for our sins. For the Apostle established this even in his own person. For affirming that Christ had come to this end, that he might save sinners, of whom he himself had been the first, what does he add? "And I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief." Thus that clemency of God, preferring the penitence of the sinner to his death, looks to the ignorant still and the as-yet unbelieving, for the freeing of whom Christ came — not to those who now know God and have learned the sacrament. But if the clemency of God befits the still ignorant and unfaithful, then surely penitence too invites that clemency to itself — that kind of penitence after the faith being preserved, which either for lighter offences will be able to obtain pardon from the bishop, or for greater and irremissible ones from God alone.

But to what point concerning Paul, when even John seems to applaud, I know not how, the other party? — as though in the Apocalypse he had plainly set forth the help of penitence for fornication, where to the angel of the Thyatirenes the Spirit charges that he has against him that he held the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, and teaches, and seduces my servants to fornicate and to eat of things sacrificed to idols. "And I gave her space of time, that she might enter upon penitence, and she will not enter upon it" — in the matter of fornication. "Behold, I will cast her into a bed, and her adulterers with her into very great affliction, unless they shall have done penitence of her works." But it is well that it accords with the apostles and the rules both of faith and of discipline. "For whether I," he says, "or they, so we preach." It concerns therefore the whole sacrament to believe nothing conceded by John which has been denied by Paul. Whoever shall have observed this equality of the Holy Spirit will be led by him into his senses. For he was a heretical woman, who had undertaken to teach what she had learned from the Nicolaitans, and who was secretly introducing it into the Church, and was deservedly urged to penitence. For who doubts that a heretic, deceived by false teaching, his lapse afterward recognized and expiated by penitence, both obtains pardon and is brought back into the Church? Whence too with us, as on a par with the heathen — nay, even above the heathen — the heretic too is admitted, being purged by the baptism of truth in both man. Or if you are sure that that woman, after the faith, while still alive, afterward breathed her last in heresy, so that you claim pardon for her from penitence not as for a heretic but as for a faithful sinner — by all means let her do penitence; but to the end of adultery, yet not so as to obtain restoration. For this will be the penitence which we too acknowledge to be owed, much more so, but which as to pardon we reserve to God. In short, that Apocalypse, in its later parts, decreed for the shameless and fornicators, as for the timid and the unbelieving and homicides and sorcerers and idolaters — such as shall have been any such in the faith — the pool of fire, without any conditional damnation. For it will not seem to savour of heathens, since it has pronounced concerning the faithful, "They who overcome shall have this inheritance, and I will be to them God, and they to me for sons"; and so subjoined, "But for the timid and unbelieving and shameless and fornicators and homicides and sorcerers and idolaters, their portion is in the pool of fire and brimstone, which is the second death." So too again: "Blessed are they who act from the precepts, that they may have power over the tree of life, and over the gates for entering into the holy city. The dogs, the sorcerers, the fornicator, the homicide — outside" — surely those who act not from the precepts. For it belongs to those to be given outside who have been within. But, "What is it to me to judge those who are without?" — this had gone before. From the epistle of John too they pluck at once. It is said, "The blood of his Son cleanses us from all offence." Always therefore, and in every way, shall we offend, if he always and from every offence cleanses us; or, if not always, then not after the faith too; and if not from offence, then not from fornication too. But whence did he set out? He had foretold God to be light, and that there is no darkness in him; and that we lie if we say we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness. "But if," he says, "we walk in the light, we shall have fellowship with him, and the blood of Jesus Christ our Lord cleanses us from all offence." Do we then, walking in the light, offend; and, offending in the light, shall we be cleansed? By no means. For he who offends is not in the light, but in darkness. Whence too he shows in what way we shall be cleansed from offence — walking in the light, in which offence cannot be done. So thoroughly does he say we are thus cleansed, not in that we offend, but in that we offend not. For walking in the light, but not communicating with the darkness, we shall act as cleansed — not by laying aside, but by not committing, the offence. For this is the force of the Lord's blood: that those whom it has already cleansed from offence, and thereafter set in the light, it should thereafter render clean, if they shall have persevered in walking in the light. "But he subjoins," you say, "If we say we have no offence, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our offences, he is faithful and just, to forgive them to us, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." Is it then from uncleanness? Or, if it is so, then also from idolatry. But something else is in the sense. For lo, again, "If we say," he says, "that we have not offended, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us." Yet more: "Little children, these things I have written to you, that you may not offend; and if you shall have offended, we have an advocate with God the Father, Jesus Christ the just, and he is the propitiation for our offences." "According to these things," you say, "it is agreed both that we offend and that we have pardon." What then shall come of it, when, going on, I find something else? For he denies that we offend at all, and treats much of this, that he may concede nothing of the kind — setting forth that offences are once for all blotted out by Christ, not afterward to have pardon — in which the sense commits us to the admonition of chastity. "Everyone," he says, "who has this hope chastens himself, even as he is chaste. Everyone who commits offence commits also iniquity, and offence is iniquity. And you know that he was manifested to take away offences" — surely such as are hitherto being admitted. Since he subjoins, "Everyone who abides in him offends not. Everyone who offends has neither seen nor known him. Little children, let no one seduce you. Everyone who does justice is just, even as he too is just. He who commits offence is of the devil, since the devil offends from the beginning. For to this end was the Son of God manifested, that he might dissolve the works of the devil." For he dissolved them too, freeing man through the laver, the handwriting of death being remitted to him. And therefore, "everyone who is born of God commits not offence, because the seed of God abides in him; and he cannot offend, because he is born of God. In this are manifest the sons of God and the sons of the devil." In what, but in that the one offend not, by which they are born of God, but the others offend, because they are of the devil — just as if they had never been born of God? But if he says, "He who is not just is not of God," he who is not modest, how shall he again become of God, who has now ceased to be? It is near at hand, therefore, to say that John fell out with himself: in the earlier part of the epistle denying that we are without offence, but now prescribing that we offend not at all; and there indeed flattering somewhat about pardon, but here strictly denying that any are sons of God who shall have offended. But far from it. For neither did we ourselves fall away from the distinction of offences from which we set out. For here too John commended it — that there are certain offences of daily incursion, to which we are all subject. For to whom will it not happen either to be angry unjustly, and beyond sunset, or even to lay hand upon another, or easily to curse, or rashly to swear, or to break the faith of a compact, or to lie from shame or necessity? In affairs, in offices, in trade, in food, in seeing, in hearing, what temptation! — so that, if there were no pardon for these things, salvation would suit no one. Of these, therefore, there will be pardon through Christ, the entreater of the Father. But there are also, against these, as graver and deadly, such as do not admit pardon: homicide, idolatry, fraud, denial, blasphemy — surely also adultery and fornication, and whatever other violation of the temple of God. For these Christ will be no further an entreater; these will not at all be admitted by him who has been born of God, who will not be a son of God if he shall have admitted them. Thus John's reasoning of the diversity stands, disposing the distinction of offences, when he now grants, now denies, that sons of God offend. For he was looking out for the closing of his letter, and was building up these senses for himself, about to say in the end more manifestly: "If anyone knows his brother to be committing a sin not unto death, he shall ask, and the Lord, who offends not unto death, shall give him life. For there is a sin unto death; I do not say of that, that one should ask." He too remembered that Jeremiah was forbidden by God to entreat for a people committing mortal offences. "All unrighteousness is offence; and there is a sin unto death. But we know that everyone who is born of God offends not" — namely the offence which is unto death. So now nothing remains but either to deny that adultery and fornication are mortal offences, or to confess them irremissible, for which it is not permitted to entreat.

The discipline therefore of the apostles instructs and determines, properly and principally, the high-priesthood of all sanctity toward the temple of God — that everywhere from the Church should be uprooted all sacrilege of modesty, without any mention of restoration. Yet I wish, out of abundance, to add over and above the testimony of some companion of the apostles too, fit to confirm, from the nearest right, the discipline of the masters. For there is extant also the writing of Barnabas, entitled "to the Hebrews" — a man sufficiently authorized by God, as one whom Paul set beside himself in the tenor of abstinence: "Or have I alone, and Barnabas, not the power of working?" And surely the epistle of Barnabas is more received among the churches than that apocryphal "Shepherd" of the adulterers. Admonishing therefore his disciples, all beginnings being omitted, to tend rather to perfection, and not again to lay the foundations of penitence from the works of the dead, he says, "For it is impossible that those who were once illuminated, and tasted the heavenly gift, and partook of the Holy Spirit, and tasted the sweet word of God — when the age is now setting, when they have fallen away — should again be recalled to penitence, crucifying again to themselves and dishonouring the Son of God. For the earth which drinks in the moisture coming often upon it, and brings forth grass apt for those for whom it is also cultivated, obtains the blessing of God; but bringing forth thorns, it is reprobate and nigh to cursing, whose end is for burning." He who learned this from the apostles, and taught it with the apostles, never knew a second penitence promised by the apostles to the adulterer and fornicator. For he most excellently interpreted the law, and preserved its figures already in the very truth. To this aspect, in short, of discipline, it was provided concerning the leper: "But if the spotting break out in the skin, and cover the whole skin from the head even to the feet through the whole sight, and the priest, when he has seen it, shall cleanse him, since it has turned all white, he is clean. But on whatever day there shall be seen in him such a colour, living, he is defiled." For he willed it to be understood that a man converted from his former habit of the flesh into the whiteness of faith — which is esteemed a vice and a spot in the world — and wholly renewed, is clean, who is now not spotted, not besprinkled from the old and the new. But if after the abolition, in the old way, anything of that has come to life again, then again in his flesh that which was held dead by offence is to be judged unclean, nor any more expiated by the priest. Thus adultery, relapsing from the old way and bespotting the unity of the new colour, from which it had been excluded, is an uncleansable vice. Likewise of the house: if any spots and hollownesses had been announced to the priest in the walls, before he should enter to inspect it, he orders all things to be taken out of the house, so that the things which should be the house's may not become unclean. Then, the priest having entered, if he had found hollownesses greening or reddening, and their aspect lower below the wall's surface, he should go out to the door and separate that house for seven days. Then, returning on the seventh day, if he had observed that touch spread through the walls, he should command those stones to be drawn out in which the touch of the leprosy had been, and cast outside the city into an unclean place, and other stones, polished and solid, to be taken and set in the place of the former, and the house to be smeared with other plaster. For it is fitting that, when one comes to the high priest, Christ the Father's — within the space of the week — there should first be taken away from the house of our man all impediments, that the house which remains may be clean — the flesh and soul; and where the word of God enters it and finds the spots of redness and greenness, that there be at once drawn out and cast forth the deadly and bloody senses (for the Apocalypse too set death upon a green horse, but a warrior upon a red one), and in place of these be laid stones polished and fitted into a framework and firm — such as are made in Abraham's — that so the man may be fit for God. But if after the recovery and reformation the priest shall again observe in the same house anything of the former causes and spots, he pronounces it unclean, and orders the materials and stones and all its structure to be laid aside and cast into an unclean place. This will be the man — flesh and soul — who after baptism and the entering of the priests, reformed, again resumes the scabbiness and spots of the flesh, and is cast outside the city into an unclean place — handed over, namely, to Satan for the destruction of the flesh — nor any more rebuilt in the Church after his ruin. So too of the concubinage of a handmaid who had been reserved for a man, not yet redeemed, not yet freed. "Provision shall be made," he says, "for her, and she shall not die, because she had not yet been freed for whom she was kept." For the flesh, not yet freed by Christ, for whom it was kept, was being defiled with impunity; but now, being freed, it has no pardon.

If the apostles knew these things better, surely they cared the more. But I will now descend to this stage too, sifting between the doctrine of the apostles and their power. Discipline governs man; power sets its seal — apart, that the power is the Spirit's, but the Spirit is God. What did he teach? That there should be no communicating with the works of darkness. Observe what he commands. But who could grant offences? This is his alone. For who remits offences but God alone? — and surely the mortal ones, which shall have been admitted against him, and against his temple. For as to the things which against you have a charge upon you, you are bidden, in the person of Peter, to forgive even seventy times seven. Therefore, even if it were agreed that the blessed apostles themselves had indulged some such thing, the pardon of which would befit them from God, not from man, they had done it not from discipline, but from power. For they both raised the dead, which God alone does, and restored the feeble to integrity, which none but Christ does; nay, they even inflicted plagues, which Christ would not. For it did not become him to rage who had come to suffer. Ananias was struck, and Elymas — Ananias by death, Elymas by blindness — that by this very thing it might be proved that Christ had been able to do these things too. So too the prophets had forgiven the slaughter, and adultery along with it, to the penitent, because they had also wrought proofs of severity. Show me therefore now too, O apostolic man, the prophetic examples, that I may acknowledge the divinity, and claim to yourself the power of remitting offences of this kind. But if you have obtained the offices of discipline alone, and to preside not by command but by ministry — who or how great are you, to indulge, who, exhibiting neither prophet nor apostle, lack that power whose it is to indulge? "But the Church," you say, "has the power of forgiving offences." This I rather both acknowledge and dispose of — I who have the Paraclete himself saying, in the new prophets, "The Church can forgive an offence, but I will not do it, lest they offend in other things too." What if a pseudo-prophetic spirit pronounced it? But it would rather have been the part of a subverter both to commend himself by clemency and to dispose the rest to delinquency. Or if even this he was eager to affect according to the spirit of truth — then the spirit of truth can indeed indulge pardon to fornicators, but, with the harm of the many, he will not. Now I ask of your view: whence do you usurp this right for the Church? If it is because the Lord said to Peter, "Upon this rock I will build my Church; to you I have given the keys of the heavenly kingdom"; or, "Whatsoever you shall bind or loose on earth shall be bound or loosed in the heavens" — do you therefore presume that the power of binding and loosing has been derived to you too — that is, to every Church akin to Peter? Of what sort are you, subverting and changing the manifest intention of the Lord, conferring this on Peter personally? "Upon you," he says, "I will build my Church"; and, "I will give you the keys" — not to the Church; and, "Whatsoever you shall loose or bind" — not what they shall loose or bind. For so too the outcome teaches. In him the Church was built up — that is, through him; he himself first handselled the key. You see what key: "Men of Israel, give ear to what I say: Jesus of Nazareth, a man destined to you by God," and the rest. He himself, in short, first unlocked, in the baptism of Christ, the entrance of the heavenly kingdom, by which are loosed the offences formerly bound, and bound those which had not been loosed, according to true salvation; and he bound Ananias with the bond of death, and loosed the man feeble in his feet from the vice of his infirmity. But also in that disputation, whether or not the law was to be kept, Peter first of all, moved by the Spirit, and speaking beforehand concerning the calling of the nations, says, "And now why do you tempt the Lord concerning the imposing of a yoke upon the brethren, which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear? But through the grace of Jesus we believe that we shall obtain salvation, as also they." This sentence both loosed those things of the law which were omitted, and bound those which were reserved. So little has the power of loosing and binding, made over to Peter, anything to do with the capital offences of the faithful. For if the Lord had enjoined upon him to indulge even a brother offending against him seventy times seven, surely he would have commanded nothing afterward to be bound — that is, retained — except perhaps such things as one may admit against the Lord, not against a brother. For it is prejudged that offences against God are not to be remitted, when those committed against a man are forgiven. What now even to the Church, and indeed to yours, O Psychic? For according to the person of Peter, this power will befit spiritual men — an apostle or a prophet. For the Church itself, properly and principally, is the Spirit himself, in whom is the Trinity of the one divinity — Father and Son and Holy Spirit. He gathers that Church which the Lord set in three. And so thereafter every number whatever that shall have conspired into this faith is reckoned a Church by its Author and Consecrator. And therefore the Church indeed will forgive offences, but the Church of the Spirit, through a spiritual man, not the Church which is a number of bishops. For the right and the decision is the Lord's, not the servant's; God's own, not the priest's.

But you now even pour out this power upon your martyrs. As soon as anyone, by agreement, has put on bonds — still soft — in the new style of imprisonment, at once the adulterers court him, at once the fornicators approach him; now prayers resound around, now tears stream around — those of every defiled person; nor do any redeem the entrance of the prison more than those who have lost the Church. Men and women are violated in the darkness, plainly known by the habit of their lusts, and they seek peace from those who are in peril concerning their own. Others flee to the mines, and thence return as communicants — where now another martyrdom is necessary for the new offences after the martyrdom. For who on earth and in the flesh is without fault? What martyr, an inhabitant of the world, is not a suppliant to coin, beholden to the physician and the moneylender? Suppose now, the head being already poised beneath the sword; suppose the body already stretched upon the cross; suppose the lion already granted at the stake; suppose the fire already heaped upon the wheel — in that very security, I say, and possession of martyrdom, who permits a man to grant what must be reserved to God — by whom these things have been damned without excuse, which not even the apostles, so far as I know, themselves martyrs, judged to be grantable? In short, Paul had already fought with the beasts at Ephesus, when he decreed destruction for the incestuous man. Let it suffice the martyr to have purged his own offences. It is the part of the ungrateful or the proud to scatter upon others too what one has obtained as a great thing. Who has loosed another's death by his own, but the Son of God alone? For even in his very passion he freed the robber. For to this end he had come, that, himself pure from offence and wholly holy, he might die for sinners. Accordingly you who emulate him by forgiving offences — if you yourself have offended in nothing, plainly suffer for me. But if you are a sinner, how shall the oil of your little torch be able to suffice both for you and for me? I have even now wherewith to prove Christ. If for this reason Christ is in the martyr, that the martyr may absolve adulterers and fornicators, let him publish the hidden things of the heart, that so he may grant offences — and he is Christ. For thus did the Lord Jesus Christ show his power: "Why do you think evil in your hearts? For which is easier — to say to the paralytic, Your sins are forgiven you, or, Rise and walk? Therefore, that you may know that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, I say to you, paralytic, Rise and walk." If the Lord cared so much about the proof of his power, that he should expose men's thoughts and so command health, lest it should not be believed that he could forgive offences — it is not lawful for me to believe the same power in anyone without the same proofs. But when you exact pardon for adulterers and fornicators from a martyr, you yourself confess that crimes of this kind are not to be washed away save by one's own martyrdom — you who presume to do it by another's. And if that is so, then martyrdom too will be another baptism. "For I have," he says, "another baptism." Whence too, from the wound of the Lord's side, water and blood flowed, the matter of either laver. I ought therefore, by the first laver too, to free another, if I can by the second; and we must of necessity drive home into the bosom: Whatever authority, whatever reason, restores ecclesiastical peace to the adulterer and fornicator, the same ought to come to the aid of the homicide and idolater too when penitent — surely of the denier; and surely of that man whom, struggling with torments in the battle of confession, savagery cast down. But it is unworthy of God and of his mercy, which prefers the penitence of the sinner to his death, that those should return more easily into the Church who fell by yielding than those who fell by fighting. Indignity urges us to say it. You will rather recall bodies that are defiled than bloodstained. What penitence is the more pitiable — that which prostrates flesh tickled, or rather torn? Which is the more just pardon, in all causes — that which the voluntary, or that which the unwilling, sinner implores? No one willing is compelled to deny; no one unwilling fornicates. There is no force toward lust but its own; it knows not how to be compelled to anything. But denial — how many devices of the executioner and kinds of punishment compel it? Who has denied the more — he who lost Christ being tormented, or he who lost him being delighted? He who grieved while he lost, or he who made sport while he lost? And yet those scars graven in the Christian battle — even invidious before Christ, because they longed to conquer, and even thus glorious, because they yielded not by conquering, but in not conquering gave way, scars at which even the devil himself still sighs — to those men, with their unhappiness, yet chaste; with their penitence, mourning but not blushing toward the Lord for pardon — to them shall pardon again be remitted, because they denied in a way that calls for expiation. To those alone is the flesh weak. And yet no flesh is so strong as that which dashes out the spirit.
